verses.1: Al-Mizan explains that the person scowled, contracted his face, and turned away because the blind man approached him.
verses.2: Al-Mizan explains that the person scowled, contracted his face, and turned away because the blind man approached him.
verses.3: Al-Mizan defines tazakkī as self-purification through good deeds, following the heed given to true beliefs; admonition benefits only by producing that belief and conduct. Thus the blind seeker may already have heeded, or may heed through seeking knowledge, and then purify himself. The change from third-person description in 80:1-2 to direct second-person rebuke in (80:3-4) intensifies censure and establishes the argument. The visitor's blindness, religious need, striving, and fear of God remove any excuse for frowning or turning away and require special care. Al-Mizan rejects the suggestion that the third person and later direct address honor the Prophet: the sharper rebuke in (80:5-6) permits neither that reading nor the supposed kindness.

verses.5: Al-Mizan reads istaghnāʾ as affluent self-sufficiency that brings social prominence and pride before truth, recalling that man becomes rebellious when he sees himself without need (96:6-7). The rebuke is that the addressee attends such arrogant people while neglecting fearful seekers of purification, even though their failure to purify does not make him responsible. Taṣaddā means turning to something with attentive care. Of three readings of mā in (80:7)—no harm if they do not purify; a rhetorical question limiting the messenger to conveying the message; or indifference to their disbelief and sin—Al-Mizan prefers the third as most fitting the surrounding reproof.

verses.8: Al-Mizan takes yasʿā to mean hastening toward admonition and purification through religious learning, while yakhshā denotes fear of God arising from such admonition, as (20:2-3) and (87:10) show. Talahhā, an elision of tatalahhā, means occupying oneself with something else. The placement of the pronouns before the verbs in 80:6 and (80:10) reinforces the rebuke.

verses.11:
Al-Mizan says kallā rejects frowning, turning away, attending the affluent, and disregarding the God-fearing. The feminine innahā may denote Qur'anic verses or the Qur'an through the feminine predicate: both are a reminder of true belief and right conduct. Voluntary remembrance is a return to fiṭrah (primordial nature, innate disposition, pristine conscience); there is no compulsion in the call, and its benefit belongs to the person who heeds.

Al-Mizan reads ṣuḥuf as honored scriptures, the plural of ṣaḥīfah, a written sheet or book, carried by angels of revelation. They are exalted and purified from falsehood, vain talk, uncertainty, and contradiction. It rejects identifying the plural with the Guarded Tablet or prior prophetic scriptures, the latter conflicting with the scriptures being in the hands of envoys. Ṣafarah means messenger-envoys: noble in essence and pious in deeds, they carry revelation as Gabriel's assistants, so their action can be ascribed to Gabriel and ultimately to God. The commentary finds readings of safarah as angelic scribes or Qur'an reciters less apparent.

verses.17: Al-Mizan treats ‘Perish man!’ as a curse prompted by human absorption in desire, forgetfulness of divine Lordship, and refusal of God's commands. Akfarahu expresses astonishment at extreme kufr, the concealment of clear truth: people know they lie under God's governance, so it includes denial of Lordship and withholding worship. Though kufr can mean thanklessness, the commentary finds the broader meaning more pertinent here. It reports al-Kashshāf's view that the paired phrases are exceptionally vehement and comprehensive censure, and prefers exclamatory mā, ‘how ungrateful,’ to the interrogative reading, ‘what made him ungrateful?’
verses.18: Al-Mizan reads the question as denying that creation gives human beings any excuse for disbelief, disobedience, or rebellion. Creator and creature are left unnamed because everyone intuitively knows that God alone created them, including the polytheists. The question heightens the astonishment at their ingratitude and prepares the answer that they came from an insignificant drop of seminal fluid, which controls neither its origin nor the direction of its life, death, and resurrection.
verses.19: Al-Mizan says the indefinite nuṭfah stresses the insignificance and abasement of the seminal drop from which God created humankind; such an origin leaves no ground for arrogant rebellion against their Lord. Fa-qaddarahu means that God subjects their essence, attributes, and actions to qadr, measure and limit. His all-encompassing direction leaves them unable independently to acquire what has not been allotted to them.
verses.20:
Al-Mizan takes the unqualified ‘way’ to be obedience to God and the path to good and happiness. It answers the objection that, if creation and proportioning determine everything, humans are compelled, cannot be blamed for kufr or sin, and cannot be subject to obligations that require free will. God’s taqdīr applies to acts through human volition: His will determines that each person acts in a particular way by free choice. People are therefore free and responsible for their acts while remaining subject to qadar.

The commentary judges less plausible the readings that the way is the infant's easy exit from the womb or that it is religious guidance and clarification of good and evil. It explains imātah as inflicting death and iqbār as burying the body, an act attributed to God because He guided and inspired people to it; it prefers this over making someone a possessor of a grave through a command to bury, since the context concerns divine direction through takwīn rather than tashrīʿ. Inshār is resurrection after death for action, and its qualification by God's will makes the resurrection sudden and unknown to anyone but Him.

verses.23: Al-Mizan says kallā answers the question raised by God's creation, direction, death, burial, and resurrection: humanity has not repaid these blessings with submission, gratitude, and obedience, but has disbelieved and disobeyed. It therefore takes ‘he has not yet carried out what He commanded him’ to refer to the human being fulfilling God's command, not to God withholding the believer's obedience merely to complete an argument; the latter is far from the apparent meaning. The rebuke concerns humanity generally through its natural propensity for kufr, but applies in fact to those who voluntarily actualize that propensity and exceed the bounds of servitude, not to all believers and unbelievers because no one worships God as He deserves.
verses.24: Al-Mizan directs every human being to observe food as one of the innumerable provisions through which God manages life, so as to recognise His extensive and delicate care for human welfare and growth. This ‘man’ differs from the person in (80:17) who has actualized kufr: it includes all people capable of reflection. The initial fāʾ marks the following account of food as a consequential elaboration of the preceding divine direction.
verses.25:
Al-Mizan reads annā, rather than innā, as continuing the command to observe food. Rain, and possibly the springs and streams ultimately formed from it, is poured down so that the earth is split by plant growth and yields human food. Thumma marks the delayed sequence from water to fissured earth, while the following fāʾ marks the immediate growth of grain.

The listed vines, vegetables, olives, palms, densely treed gardens, and fruits are human food; ghaḍb is fresh cut vegetables or herbs, though it has also been read as animal fodder, and fākihah includes fruits generally, with the named fruits receiving special attention. Abb means pasture. The plants are made as sustenance for people and their livestock; the shift to direct address underscores God's favor in directing their affairs.

verses.33: Al-Mizan identifies al-ṣākhkhah as the deafening cry of the Trumpet, the end point of God's direction of human affairs, when everyone receives the full result of obedience or disobedience. On that Day people flee even their closest relatives—not because those ties are unimportant, but because calamity and each person's own predicament absorb them so completely that they cannot attend to anyone else. Other proposed reasons lack evidence.

verses.38: Al-Mizan says the closing verses divide people into the felicitous and the wretched, whose faces disclose their condition. Musfirah means brightness and radiance caused by joy, while mustabshirah means beaming happiness at the glad tidings they behold.

verses.40: Al-Mizan defines ghabarah as dust and darkness on the face, expressing grief and sorrow; gloom then covers and envelops those faces. The contrasted complexions of 80:38-41 reveal the two groups' inward joy or sorrow because the face mirrors the heart.
verses.41: Al-Mizan defines ghabarah as dust and darkness on the face, expressing grief and sorrow; gloom then covers and envelops those faces. The contrasted complexions of 80:38-41 reveal the two groups' inward joy or sorrow because the face mirrors the heart.
verses.42: Al-Mizan identifies the wretched group as those combining unbelief in conviction with fujūr, detestable disobedience in deed; it also allows the sense of people ungrateful for God's blessings and given to mischief. The felicitous group receives no matching description because the passage's purpose is warning and admonition focused on the wretched.
